title: The Tortoise and the Hare
author: Aesop
description: A slow tortoise races a fast hare — and wins. One of the world's most famous fables about pride, patience, and persistence.
summary:
Once upon a time, a hare was very proud of how fast he could run. He often laughed at a tortoise who walked very slowly.

"You are so slow!" the hare said one day. "How do you ever get anywhere?"

The tortoise smiled quietly. "Why don't we have a race?" he said.

The hare laughed loudly. "A race? You want to race me? All right then. I agree!"

All the animals in the forest came to watch. A fox stood at the start of the road. "Ready, steady, go!" he shouted.

The hare ran as fast as the wind. In just a few minutes, he was far ahead of the tortoise. He looked back and could not even see the tortoise.

"This is too easy," the hare said to himself. "I have so much time. I will rest here under this tree for a while."

He lay down in the warm sunshine and closed his eyes. Very soon, he was fast asleep.

Meanwhile, the tortoise kept walking. One step, then another, then another. He never stopped. He never rested. He walked slowly but steadily all the way down the road.

The tortoise passed the sleeping hare. He kept on walking. Slowly, slowly, he came closer and closer to the finish line.

Finally, the tortoise crossed the finish line. All the animals cheered.

The noise woke up the hare. He jumped to his feet and ran as fast as he could. But it was too late. The tortoise was already at the finish line, smiling happily.

"How did you win?" the hare asked, very surprised.

"Slow and steady wins the race," said the tortoise.

Moral: It is better to work slowly and carefully than to rush and give up.

title: The Fox and the Grapes
author: Aesop
description: A hungry fox cannot reach a bunch of grapes and decides they must be sour anyway. A short, classic fable about self-deception.
summary:
One hot summer day, a fox was walking through a vineyard. He saw a beautiful bunch of grapes hanging high up on a vine. The grapes were large and dark purple. They looked delicious.

"Those grapes look wonderful," the fox said. "I must have them!"

He jumped up to reach the grapes. But they were too high. He tried again. Still too high. He tried a third time, and a fourth time, and a fifth time. Each time, the grapes were just out of his reach.

Finally, the fox stopped trying. He was tired and a little embarrassed. He turned away from the grapes and walked off with his nose in the air.

"I didn't really want those grapes anyway," he said to himself. "They are probably sour and unpleasant."

But of course, the grapes were not sour at all.

Moral: It is easy to pretend you don't want something you cannot have.

title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
author: Aesop
description: A shepherd boy cries wolf as a joke — until a real wolf arrives and nobody believes him. A timeless fable about honesty and trust.
summary:
There was once a young shepherd boy who looked after his flock of sheep on a hillside near a village. Every day, he sat on the hill and watched the sheep eat grass. It was quiet and a little boring.

One day, the boy had an idea for some fun. He ran down the hill toward the village, shouting as loudly as he could.

"Wolf! Wolf! There is a wolf attacking the sheep!"

The villagers heard him and ran up the hill with sticks and tools to help. But when they got there, they found no wolf — only the boy laughing.

"There is no wolf," he said, laughing at them. "I was only joking!"

The villagers were angry, but they went back to the village.

A few days later, the boy was bored again. Once more he ran down the hill, shouting "Wolf! Wolf!"

Again the villagers ran up to help. Again there was no wolf. This time, the villagers were very angry.

Then, one afternoon, a real wolf came out of the forest. It ran toward the sheep. The boy was terrified. He screamed and shouted, "Wolf! Wolf! Please help me! There really is a wolf!"

But the villagers heard him and shook their heads. "It is just that boy again," they said. Nobody came.

The wolf scattered the sheep and disappeared into the forest.

Moral: Nobody believes a liar, even when they are telling the truth.

title: The Lion and the Mouse
author: Aesop
description: A tiny mouse saves a mighty lion from a hunter's net. A beautiful fable about kindness and how even the smallest friend can help.
summary:
One day, a great lion was sleeping in the forest. A little mouse was running around and accidentally ran across the lion's nose. The lion woke up with a roar and caught the mouse in his enormous paw.

"How dare you wake me up!" the lion growled. "I shall eat you!"

"Please, Your Majesty, let me go!" the mouse cried. "I did not mean to wake you. If you spare my life, I promise I will help you one day!"

The lion looked at the tiny mouse and started to laugh. "You — help me? That is very funny! What could a little creature like you ever do for me?" But he felt kind, so he opened his paw and let the mouse go free.

Some weeks later, the lion was walking in the forest when he stepped into a hunter's net. He was trapped. He struggled and pulled, but the ropes were too strong. He let out a great roar of frustration.

The little mouse heard the roar and ran to find the lion. He saw the lion trapped in the net.

"I remember you!" the mouse cried. "You showed me kindness. Now I will help you!"

The mouse began to chew through the ropes with his sharp teeth. One by one, the ropes broke. Very soon, the lion was free.

"Thank you, little friend," the lion said humbly. "I was wrong to laugh at you."

Moral: Even the smallest friend can be a great help. No act of kindness is ever wasted.

title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
author: Aesop
description: An ant works hard all summer while a grasshopper plays music. When winter comes, only one of them is prepared. A classic fable about hard work and planning ahead.
summary:
On a warm summer's day, a grasshopper was sitting in a meadow, playing his violin and singing happily. He watched a line of ants walking past, each carrying a large grain of wheat.

"Why are you working so hard on such a beautiful day?" the grasshopper asked. "Come and sing with me!"

"We are storing food for the winter," said one ant, without stopping. "You should do the same."

"Winter is a long time away," the grasshopper laughed. "There is plenty of food now. I would rather enjoy the sunshine."

The ants kept working, day after day. They carried seeds and grain to their underground home. The grasshopper kept playing and singing all summer long.

Then autumn came. The leaves turned red and gold and fell from the trees. The air became cold. The grasshopper noticed that the meadow was looking empty, but he was not worried.

Then winter arrived. Snow covered the ground. The grasshopper looked everywhere for food but could find nothing. He was cold and very hungry.

He went to the ants' home and knocked on the door. "Please," he said, "could you share a little food with me? I am starving."

An ant came to the door and looked at him. "What were you doing all summer while we were working?" she asked.

"I was playing music and singing," the grasshopper said quietly.

"Then you must sing through the winter too," the ant replied, and closed the door.

Moral: It is wise to prepare today for the needs of tomorrow.

title: The Crow and the Pitcher
author: Aesop
description: A thirsty crow finds a pitcher with only a little water at the bottom. Unable to reach it, the crow uses clever thinking to solve the problem.
summary:
On a very hot day, a thirsty crow was flying over a dry landscape, looking for water. After a long search, the crow spotted a tall water pitcher sitting outside a house.

The crow flew down and looked inside the pitcher. There was water at the bottom — but not very much. The pitcher was tall and narrow, and the water level was far too low for the crow to reach with its beak.

The crow tried to tip the pitcher over, but it was too heavy. He tried to break it, but it was too strong. He sat beside the pitcher and thought carefully.

Then the crow had an idea. He looked around and saw small pebbles on the ground.

One by one, the crow picked up the pebbles in his beak and dropped them into the pitcher. After each pebble, the water level rose just a tiny bit. He kept working, dropping pebble after pebble.

Slowly, slowly, the water rose higher and higher in the pitcher. At last, the water was close enough for the crow to dip his beak in and drink.

The crow drank deeply and flew away, satisfied.

Moral: Necessity is the mother of invention. Think carefully and use what you have.

title: The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs
author: Aesop
description: A farmer discovers his goose lays golden eggs — one a day. When greed takes over, he makes a terrible decision he cannot undo.
summary:
Once there was a farmer and his wife who owned a very ordinary goose. One morning, when the farmer went to collect eggs from the nest, he found something extraordinary. Instead of a normal white egg, there was a shining, heavy egg of pure gold.

The farmer could hardly believe it. He brought the egg inside and had it tested. It was real gold.

The next morning, the goose laid another golden egg. And the morning after that, another. Every single day, the goose laid one perfect golden egg.

The farmer and his wife became rich. They sold the golden eggs at the market and used the money to buy fine clothes, a bigger house, and beautiful furniture.

But soon, the farmer became impatient. "Why should I wait for one egg a day?" he said to his wife. "If we cut open the goose, we can get all the golden eggs at once!"

His wife thought this was a wonderful idea. The next morning, the farmer took a knife and cut open the goose.

But inside the goose, there were no golden eggs — none at all. It was just an ordinary goose inside. And now it was dead.

The golden eggs were gone forever.

Moral: Greed can destroy what is good. Those who want too much may end up with nothing at all.

title: The North Wind and the Sun
author: Aesop
description: The North Wind and the Sun compete to remove a traveller's coat. One uses force, the other uses warmth. A fable about persuasion versus power.
summary:
One day, the North Wind and the Sun were having an argument about which of them was stronger.

"I am clearly stronger," said the North Wind. "I can blow down trees and create giant storms at sea."

"Strength is not only about force," said the Sun calmly. "I believe I am stronger than you."

Just then, they saw a traveller walking along a road below them. The traveller was wearing a long, warm coat.

"Let us have a contest," said the Sun. "The one who can make that traveller remove his coat is the stronger of us."

The North Wind agreed. "I will go first," he said.

The North Wind took a deep breath and blew as hard as he could. A powerful, icy blast swept down toward the traveller. The traveller felt the cold wind and immediately pulled his coat tighter around himself. He held it closed with both hands and leaned forward into the wind.

The harder the North Wind blew, the tighter the traveller held his coat. Finally, the North Wind gave up, exhausted.

"Now it is my turn," said the Sun.

The Sun came out from behind a cloud and shone with gentle warmth. The traveller felt the pleasant heat and relaxed. After a few more steps, he unbuttoned his coat. A little later, he took it off completely and carried it over his arm.

"You see," said the Sun, smiling, "gentleness and warmth are more powerful than force."

Moral: Persuasion is more effective than force.

title: The Three Little Pigs
author: Traditional
description: Three pigs each build a house from different materials. When the Big Bad Wolf comes to blow them down, only the strongest house survives.
summary:
Once upon a time, there were three little pigs who left home to build their own houses. Their mother warned them to be careful of the Big Bad Wolf.

The first little pig was in a hurry. He quickly built a house from straw. "This is easy!" he said. "I still have lots of time to play."

The second little pig built his house from sticks. It took a little longer, but soon it was done. "Good enough!" he said, and went off to play with his brother.

The third little pig worked hard for many days, building his house from bricks. His brothers laughed at him. "You're working too hard!" they said. "Come and play with us!" But the third pig kept working until his house was strong and solid.

That evening, the Big Bad Wolf came out of the forest. He was very hungry. He came to the house of straw first.

"Little pig, little pig, let me come in!" he howled.

"No, no, not by the hair of my chinny chin chin!" cried the first little pig.

"Then I'll huff, and I'll puff, and I'll blow your house in!" said the wolf.

And he huffed and he puffed and he blew the straw house right down. The first little pig ran as fast as he could to his brother's house of sticks.

The wolf followed him there. "Little pigs, little pigs, let me come in!"

"No, no, not by the hair of our chinny chin chins!"

"Then I'll huff, and I'll puff, and I'll blow your house in!"

And he huffed and he puffed and he blew the stick house down too. The two little pigs ran to their brother's brick house.

The wolf followed them and knocked on the strong brick door. "Little pigs, little pigs, let me come in!"

"No, no, not by the hair of our chinny chin chins!"

"Then I'll huff, and I'll puff, and I'll blow your house in!"

The wolf huffed and puffed. He puffed and huffed. But no matter how hard he blew, the brick house did not move. He tried again and again, but the house was too strong.

Finally, the wolf climbed up onto the roof to come down the chimney. But the third little pig had lit a fire in the fireplace below. The wolf came down the chimney, felt the heat, and jumped back out. He ran away into the forest and never came back.

The three little pigs lived happily and safely in the brick house.

Moral: Hard work and careful preparation protect you from danger.

title: Little Red Riding Hood
author: Brothers Grimm
description: A girl in a red cloak visits her sick grandmother in the forest — but a cunning wolf arrives first. A classic tale of deception, danger, and courage.
summary:
Once upon a time, there was a sweet little girl who was loved by everyone who knew her. Her grandmother had given her a beautiful red velvet cloak with a hood, and the girl loved it so much that she wore it everywhere. Because of this, everyone called her Little Red Riding Hood.

One day, Little Red Riding Hood's mother said, "Your grandmother is not feeling well. Please take her this basket of food — some bread, butter, and a bottle of wine. Stay on the path through the forest and do not talk to strangers."

Little Red Riding Hood promised to be careful and set off into the forest.

The forest was beautiful and quiet. But a cunning wolf was watching from behind the trees. He wanted to eat Little Red Riding Hood, but he could hear woodcutters working nearby. So instead he approached her.

"Good morning, Little Red Riding Hood," the wolf said pleasantly. "Where are you going on such a lovely day?"

"I am going to my grandmother's house," she said, forgetting her promise. "She lives in the house near the old oak tree on the other side of the forest."

"How kind you are!" said the wolf. "I know a shortcut — look at all those lovely flowers you could pick for her along the path."

While Little Red Riding Hood stopped to pick flowers, the wolf ran ahead on the shortcut to Grandmother's house. He knocked on the door.

"Who is there?" called the grandmother.

"It is Little Red Riding Hood, bringing you food," the wolf said, disguising his voice.

"Lift the latch and come in, dear," said the grandmother.

The wolf came in and swallowed the grandmother whole. He put on her nightcap and glasses and got into her bed to wait.

When Little Red Riding Hood arrived, she knocked and entered. She walked toward the bed but something seemed strange.

"Grandmother, what big ears you have!"
"All the better to hear you with, my dear."
"What big eyes you have!"
"All the better to see you with, my dear."
"What big teeth you have!"
"All the better to EAT you with!"

The wolf leapt out of bed. Little Red Riding Hood screamed. Fortunately, a huntsman was passing by and heard her cry. He burst through the door and overpowered the wolf. He cut open the wolf's stomach and the grandmother climbed out, shaken but alive.

Little Red Riding Hood had learned her lesson: always stay on the safe path, and never tell strangers where you are going.

Moral: Listen to your parents' warnings and be careful who you trust.

title: The Ugly Duckling
author: Hans Christian Andersen
description: A duckling is rejected by everyone for looking different. After a lonely year, he discovers he was never a duck at all — but a beautiful swan.
summary:
It was summer, and the countryside was warm and golden. In the reeds beside the river, a mother duck sat on her nest, waiting for her eggs to hatch.

One by one, the eggs cracked open. Little yellow ducklings tumbled out, stretching their wings and blinking in the sunlight. But the last egg was the largest, and it took the longest to hatch. When the shell finally broke, out came a duckling quite different from the others — grey, awkward, and unusually large.

"What a strange-looking creature," the other animals said when they saw him. "He is far too big and ugly to be a duckling."

Even the other ducklings made fun of him. They pecked at him and pushed him away. The hens ignored him. The farm dog growled at him.

The poor ugly duckling was miserable. He had no friends, and no one wanted him near. Finally, he decided to run away. He crept through the reeds and waddled off alone across the fields.

He came to a marsh where wild ducks lived. "You are very ugly," the wild ducks told him honestly, "but you may stay here if you like."

For a while, the duckling stayed in the marsh. But hunters came, and their dogs frightened him away. He ran and ran until he reached an old cottage at the edge of the forest.

An old woman let him stay, hoping he might lay eggs. But he could not. The cat and the hen who lived there looked down on him.

"Can you lay eggs?" the hen asked.

"No," said the duckling.

"Then you are completely useless," she said.

The duckling left the cottage and found a quiet lake. Autumn came, then the long, bitter winter. Ice spread across the lake, and the duckling suffered terribly from the cold. A kind farmer found him nearly frozen and carried him home, but the farmer's noisy children frightened the duckling, and he escaped again into the dark winter night.

All alone, the ugly duckling survived the winter. It was very hard.

But at last, spring came. The ice melted. Flowers appeared. The duckling felt his body had changed — he was bigger, his wings were wider.

He flew through the air — he could fly! He landed on a beautiful lake and saw a group of graceful white birds swimming toward him.

He bowed his head, expecting them to chase him away. But when he looked at his reflection in the still water, he gasped. Looking back at him was not an ugly grey duckling, but a beautiful white swan.

The other swans welcomed him warmly, and he swam among them with joy.

"I never imagined such happiness when I was the ugly duckling," he thought. "But the unhappy times only make this moment more wonderful."

Moral: Beauty and worth cannot be seen straight away. Those who suffer and are different may become the most extraordinary of all.

title: Cinderella
author: Charles Perrault
description: A kind girl is treated as a servant by her stepfamily but is transformed for one magical night at the royal ball. A beloved fairy tale about kindness and hope.
summary:
Once there was a gentleman who had a daughter with a sweet and gentle heart. After his first wife died, he married again — a proud and cold woman who had two daughters of her own. These daughters were just as unkind as their mother.

When the gentleman died, his daughter's life became very hard. Her stepmother made her do all the housework — sweeping the floors, washing the dishes, scrubbing the hearth, and cooking the meals. At night, the girl had nowhere to sleep but beside the cold fireplace, among the cinders and ash. Because of this, her stepsisters gave her a cruel nickname: Cinderella.

Despite everything, Cinderella never became bitter. She worked quietly and remained kind.

One day, an invitation arrived at the house. The king's son, the Prince, was holding a grand ball at the royal palace — and every young woman in the kingdom was invited.

The stepsisters were overjoyed. They spent days choosing beautiful dresses, ribbons, and jewels. Cinderella helped them dress, though they only laughed at her. "You — go to the ball? Don't be ridiculous!"

When they had gone, Cinderella sat alone by the fireplace and wept quietly. Then something magical happened. A bright light filled the room, and a kind old woman appeared — Cinderella's fairy godmother.

"Dry your tears," she said gently. "You shall go to the ball."

With a wave of her wand, the fairy godmother turned a pumpkin into a golden carriage, mice into horses, and rags into a magnificent silk gown. On Cinderella's feet appeared the most beautiful glass slippers ever made.

"You must leave the ball before midnight," the fairy godmother warned. "When the clock strikes twelve, everything will return to as it was."

At the palace, everyone turned to look at the beautiful stranger. The Prince noticed her immediately and danced with her all evening. Cinderella had never been so happy.

Then the clock began to strike midnight. Dong! Dong! Cinderella remembered the warning and ran. She fled down the palace steps so quickly that one of her glass slippers fell off. The Prince called after her, but she disappeared into the dark.

All that was left on the palace steps was a single glass slipper.

The Prince was determined to find the young woman he had danced with. He sent messengers throughout the kingdom with the slipper, trying it on the foot of every young woman. None could make it fit.

When the messenger came to Cinderella's house, her stepsisters tried desperately to squeeze their feet into the tiny slipper. Neither could.

Then Cinderella asked quietly if she might try. Her stepsisters laughed. But the slipper slipped onto Cinderella's foot perfectly. Then she reached into her pocket and produced the matching slipper.

The Prince found her and, recognising her, asked her to marry him. Cinderella forgave her stepsisters and left with the Prince to begin a new, happy life at the palace.

Moral: Kindness and goodness are rewarded. Beauty of character matters more than beauty of appearance.
